title: Consistency per feature, and the levels between strong and eventual
dek: Real systems rarely choose consistency or availability once for everything. A ticketing app needs strict consistency for booking a seat and none for showing the match preview; a dating app needs it for a match and not for a profile photo. And between 'strong' and 'eventual' there are levels that fix most of what users notice for much less cost. This is where senior answers go beyond the one-line CAP choice.

items: Decide per feature, and say it in one sentence: 'consistency for booking seats, availability for browsing matches.'

Between strong and eventual: causal consistency (effects never appear before their causes), and read-your-own-writes (you always see your own changes). Both are cheaper than strong and fix most visible glitches.
The single test: 'Does every read need to see the latest write?' If yes, consistency; if not, availability, with the weakest level users won't notice.

body.x: Most products contain features of both kinds. Two examples:

items: A cricket ticketing app. Booking a seat needs strong consistency, so no seat is sold twice. Viewing the match page, the teams, the venue, the preview, can favour availability: a description that is a minute out of date harms nobody. In an interview: 'For this ticketing system I'll keep booking strongly consistent and let browsing favour availability.'

A dating app. A match needs consistency: if two people swipe right on each other at almost the same moment, both should see the match, once. Viewing a profile can favour availability: an old photo for a minute after it changed is fine. In an interview: 'Consistency for matching, availability for viewing profiles.'

body.cap: One ticketing app, two choices: booking a seat goes through one consistent store and may refuse during a split; browsing matches is served by replicas and caches and keeps working.

body.x: Zotato is the same: placing an order and paying need consistency; menus, ratings and search favour availability. Splitting the system by feature this way is normal, and saying it explicitly is what interviewers look for at senior level.

body.cap: During a split between Mumbai and Hyderabad, a wallet top-up is refused because the balance can't be confirmed, while a menu edit is accepted and merged later: two features, two choices, in one system.

body.x: When people say 'consistency' in CAP, they mean strong consistency. But there is a range between strong and eventual, and the levels in the middle often give users what they need for much less cost:

items: Strong consistency: every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. The most expensive in latency and availability, and necessary where exactness matters: account balances, seat bookings, stock.

Causal consistency: if one event caused another, everyone sees them in that order. A reply never appears before the comment it answers; a 'delivered' status never shows before 'picked up'. Unrelated events may appear in different orders to different people.

Read-your-own-writes: you always see your own changes immediately, even if others see them a little later. After you edit your profile you see the new version, which is what users actually notice. Common in social and content products.

Eventual consistency: if writes stop, all copies eventually agree; until then a read may be old. The weakest and cheapest, and the default of many distributed databases. DNS is the classic example: a changed record reaches everyone within minutes or hours. It is what you get when you choose availability.

body.cap: A biryani's price changes from ₹250 to ₹280 at 100 ms. A strong read shows ₹280 at once, and so does the owner reading their own change; a customer on a lagging replica sees the old price for a while, and one bouncing between replicas can even see it go backwards.

body.x: CAP matters because it sets the direction of the design, and it shouldn't be skipped. But it doesn't need to be complicated. For each feature ask: 'Does every read need to see the most recent write?' If yes, prioritise consistency. If not, prioritise availability, and pick the weakest level of consistency your users won't notice.

items: Split the system by feature and give each its choice in one sentence.
Use the middle levels: read-your-own-writes for a user's own changes, causal for conversations and status updates.
Close with the one question, applied to the system in front of you.
